questions.q: In the backtest, minimum-variance had the highest return, lowest volatility, best Sharpe, AND shallowest drawdown all at once. What is the correct conclusion to draw from this?
options: This is one simulated path -- it is NOT strong enough evidence to conclude minimum-variance is structurally superior to the other methods
Minimum-variance is now proven to be the best portfolio construction method in all cases
Tangency and risk-parity must contain calculation errors, since min-variance dominated on every metric
The result should be trusted exactly as computed with no further scrutiny
questions.explain: One realized path is a single noisy draw from a distribution of possible outcomes -- a clean sweep on one path is not evidence of structural superiority, especially given how small the asset universe and path count are here.

questions.q: The tangency portfolio was built using the exact TRUE expected returns (mu) in this simulation, yet it underperformed minimum-variance on this backtest. Why isn't this a contradiction?
options: Tangency maximizes EXPECTED Sharpe ratio across many possible paths, but any single realized path is still just one noisy draw that can deviate from that expectation
The tangency formula must have been implemented incorrectly
This proves tangency weights are always wrong
Using the true mu value guarantees the best realized outcome on every single backtest
questions.explain: Expected-value optimality does not guarantee the best outcome on any one specific realized path -- that's exactly the kind of sampling noise that can make a theoretically optimal method underperform on a single draw.

questions.q: What is the only honest way to tell whether minimum-variance is structurally better than tangency, rather than just having gotten lucky on one simulated path?
options: Rerun the backtest across many different random seeds / paths and compare the AVERAGE ranking and the SPREAD of outcomes, not just one path's result
Trust whichever method won the single available backtest
Increase the number of assets in the portfolio until the result changes
There is no way to ever determine which method is structurally better
questions.explain: Running many independent paths and looking at the average and the spread of outcomes is the only way to separate genuine structural performance from one lucky (or unlucky) random draw.

questions.q: How does this lesson's skepticism connect back to Chapter 4's data snooping and overfitting lesson?
options: Both warn against drawing strong conclusions from a single result on one finite sample, whether that sample is a backtested trading signal's Sharpe ratio or one simulated portfolio path's performance
They are unrelated topics that happen to appear in the same course
Chapter 4's lesson only applies to trading signals, never to portfolio construction
Data snooping is impossible when using true, known parameters instead of estimated ones
questions.explain: The same underlying statistical caution -- one noisy sample isn't strong evidence -- applies whether you're evaluating a trading rule's backtested Sharpe or a portfolio method's realized performance on one simulated path.

questions.q: Why is risk parity (Lesson 37) described as a genuinely defensible alternative specifically when return forecasts are weak?
options: Risk parity requires no expected-return (mu) estimate at all, so it cannot be led astray by a wrong or noisy mu the way mean-variance optimization can
Risk parity always produces higher returns than mean-variance optimization
Risk parity is mathematically identical to the tangency portfolio
Risk parity requires more historical data than mean-variance optimization, making it more reliable
questions.explain: Because risk parity depends only on volatilities (and correlations in the full version), it sidesteps the specific vulnerability of mean-variance optimization: sensitivity to an expected-return input that is hard to estimate reliably.
